Sensitivity analysis quantifies how much the prediction changes when individual features are altered (e.g., age or workclass), revealing which features are most critical in the misclassification of 23941. Together, they offer both interpretability and empirical insight into the model's decision boundaries.

result.explanation: Individuals 21762, 21701, and 42694 are correctly classified as <=50K due to combinations of younger age, lower education levels, and workclass/occupation patterns commonly associated with lower income brackets. For instance, individual 21762 has a young age (19), low education (10th grade, education-num=6), and is unmarried (relationship=Unmarried), which may correlate with limited income-generating capacity. Individual 21701, though older (age=45), has a low education level (HS-grad, education-num=9) and works in a low-wage occupation (Farming-fishing), with a married spouse, suggesting household stability but limited earnings potential. Individual 42694 has moderate age (23), some college education (education-num=10), and works in a craft-repair occupation—an occupation typically associated with moderate income—despite being unmarried. All three cases lack features associated with high-income groups such as high hours-per-week, high fnlwgt, or high capital gains. In contrast, individual 23941, though having similar education (some-college, education-num=10) and marital status (Married-civ-spouse), has a significantly older age (64), a very high fnlwgt (239,450), and is in a sales occupation—a role with potential for higher income and upward mobility. The high fnlwgt value, which strongly correlates with income in the dataset, may have disproportionately influenced the model’s decision, pulling it toward the >50K class despite the individual's true label. This highlights a potential bias in the model where high wealth indicators (like fnlwgt) dominate over demographic or occupational features. In TabNN, such feature interactions may be learned through attention mechanisms that weigh variance or historical frequency, leading to misclassification when high-impact features override contextual signals. Thus, the misclassification of 23941 is likely due to the model’s sensitivity to high fnlwgt and sales occupation, which are strongly linked to >50K in training data, even when other features suggest <=50K.
